title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2017 (arXiv:1608.04644)

pages.title: How strong is the strongest attack?
pages.subtitle: Building attacks to honestly measure robustness

blocks.html: The point of this page: a defense is only as convincing as the attack it survives. If you test a model against a weak attack and it holds up, you have learned almost nothing. This paper sets out to build the strongest possible attacks, so that surviving them is real evidence of robustness.

Quick shared vocabulary (used throughout this collection). An adversarial example is an input perturbed by a tiny, deliberately chosen amount $\delta$ so the model misclassifies it while a human sees no change. The distance metric measures how big $\delta$ is: the $\ell_2$ norm caps its total Euclidean length, the $\ell_0$ “norm” counts how many pixels changed at all, and the $\ell_\infty$ norm caps the largest change to any single pixel. A targeted attack forces a specific wrong label $t$; an untargeted one just wants any wrong label.

The concrete target. The defense in the crosshairs is defensive distillation (Papernot et al.), which had been reported to crush existing attacks from a 95% success rate down to 0.5% — and was being held up as a strong defense. The authors construct three new attacks, one each for $\ell_2$, $\ell_0$, and $\ell_\infty$, and show that defensive distillation provides essentially no protection: their attacks succeed 100% of the time on both the original and the distilled network, with only a marginal increase in distortion.

Why it matters. The lasting contribution is not breaking one defense. It is a careful, optimization-based methodology for crafting minimal-distortion adversarial examples that became the de facto benchmark for evaluating every defense that came after. When later papers say “we evaluated against C&W,” this is the attack they mean.
We construct three new attacks ... that are successful on both distilled and undistilled neural networks with 100% probability.

pages.title: What the attacker is allowed to do
pages.subtitle: White-box access and untargeted vs targeted goals

blocks.html: The question this page answers: before measuring an attack, you must pin down what the attacker can see and what counts as success. Vague threat models are how weak defenses look strong.

Access. The paper assumes the strongest reasonable attacker: white-box, meaning full knowledge of the model — architecture, weights, and the ability to compute gradients. This is deliberate. If you want to argue a defense is robust, you should test it against an attacker who knows everything; surviving a white-box attack is far stronger evidence than surviving a black-box one.
Targeted vs. untargeted. The authors define three flavors of misclassification goal, in increasing difficulty for the attacker:

items: Average case: pick a target class $t$ uniformly at random and force the model to output it — a representative, middle-difficulty target.
Best case: try every wrong target and report the easiest one to reach — the most favorable for the attacker, lower-bounding distortion.
Worst case: try every wrong target and report the hardest one — the most pessimistic, the truest test of a defense.

blocks.html: Concrete example. On MNIST, “average case” might mean turning a handwritten 7 into a randomly chosen target like “3”; “worst case” would find the single hardest target for that 7 (maybe “5”) and report how much distortion that took. A defense that only resists the easy targets is not robust.

Why it matters. Reporting all three cases (rather than cherry-picking the best) is part of what made this paper a methodological landmark. It refuses to let a defense hide behind favorable targets — a discipline the obfuscated-gradients paper later turned into a checklist.

pages.title: Adversarial examples as constrained optimization
pages.subtitle: Find the smallest change that flips the label

blocks.html: The intuition. We want the smallest change that fools the model. “Smallest” and “fools” are both precise, so the whole task can be written as a constrained optimization problem: among all perturbations $\delta$ that flip the label to a chosen target $t$, find the one with the smallest size.

blocks.tex: \min_{\delta} \; D(x, x+\delta) \quad \text{such that} \quad C(x+\delta) = t \;,\; x+\delta \in [0,1]^n

blocks.html: Term by term: $x$ is the clean image (a vector in $[0,1]^n$, $n$ pixels, each scaled to 0–1); $\delta$ is the perturbation we are searching for; $D(\cdot,\cdot)$ is the distance metric ($\ell_2$, $\ell_0$, or $\ell_\infty$) we want to keep small; $C(\cdot)$ is the classifier's predicted label; $t$ is the target class; and the last constraint $x+\delta \in [0,1]^n$ says the result must still be a valid image (no pixel below 0 or above 1).

Why this is hard. The constraint $C(x+\delta)=t$ is brutal for a gradient optimizer: $C$ is an argmax over the logits, so it is flat almost everywhere (gradient zero) and jumps discontinuously at decision boundaries. You cannot descend a function that has no useful slope. The entire method that follows is a sequence of moves to convert this awkward, non-differentiable problem into one Adam can actually solve.

Context. Earlier work (Szegedy et al.) solved a version of this with L-BFGS; FGSM (also in this collection) took the opposite extreme — one cheap step, no minimization. C&W sits in between in spirit but pushes the optimization much harder, which is why it finds dramatically smaller perturbations.

pages.title: Moving the constraint into the objective
pages.subtitle: A differentiable surrogate for 'is misclassified'

blocks.html: The first move. Replace the hard, non-differentiable constraint $C(x+\delta)=t$ with a soft penalty $f$ that is small (non-positive) exactly when the image is classified as $t$, and add it to the objective with a weight $c$:

Term by term: $\|\delta\|_2$ is the size of the perturbation we want small; $f(x+\delta)$ is the surrogate that drives misclassification (defined below); and $c > 0$ trades off the two goals — large $c$ prioritizes fooling the model, small $c$ prioritizes a tiny perturbation. We now minimize a single differentiable function instead of juggling a hard constraint.

Choosing $c$. Too small and the attack fails (the perturbation term dominates and never flips the label); too large and you waste distortion (you overshoot deep into the target region). The authors find the best $c$ by binary search: the smallest $c$ that still yields a successful attack. This is what keeps the final perturbation minimal — it spends exactly enough budget to cross the boundary and no more.

The surrogate $f$. The authors tried seven candidate functions for $f$ and found the best operates on the logits $Z$ (the pre-softmax scores), comparing the target logit against the strongest competing logit:

Term by term: $Z(x')_i$ is the logit for class $i$; $\max_{i\ne t} Z(x')_i$ is the largest logit among all the wrong-from-the-attacker's-view classes (i.e. not the target); subtracting $Z(x')_t$ gives the gap by which the best competitor beats the target. When the target already wins, this gap is negative and the example is misclassified-as-$t$. The outer $\max(\cdot, -\kappa)$ stops pushing once the target wins by a margin of $\kappa$.

What $\kappa$ buys you. $\kappa \ge 0$ is a confidence margin. With $\kappa = 0$ the attack stops the instant the target barely wins (minimal distortion). Raising $\kappa$ forces the example deeper into the target region, producing higher-confidence adversarial examples that transfer better to other models — at the cost of more distortion. This single knob later became the standard way to trade distortion for black-box transferability.

The remaining problem. We still have the box constraint $x+\delta \in [0,1]^n$. The naive fix is to clip pixels back into $[0,1]$ after each gradient step. But clipping wastes the optimizer's effort: the gradient may keep pushing a pixel past 1, and clipping silently discards that work every step, so the optimizer keeps fighting the wall instead of finding a better solution elsewhere.
The fix: a change of variables. Instead of optimizing pixels directly, optimize an unconstrained variable $w$ and squash it through $\tanh$ so the result is always a valid pixel:

Term by term: $w_i$ is a new free variable (any real number); $\tanh(w_i) \in (-1, 1)$; adding 1 and halving maps it smoothly to $(0, 1)$, the valid pixel range. So every value of $w$ — whatever Adam does to it — produces a legal image automatically. No clipping, no wasted steps.

Why this matters so much. Because $\tanh$ smoothly saturates near the boundaries, the optimizer gets clean gradients everywhere and can run a strong method (Adam) for many iterations. This single reparameterization is a large part of why C&W finds perturbations far smaller than clipping-based attacks — it never throws optimizer work away.

items: Surrogate $f$ on logits, not softmax probabilities — this is what sidesteps defensive distillation.
Binary search over $c$ to find the minimum-distortion success.
tanh reparameterization to satisfy the box constraint smoothly.
Adam as the inner optimizer, many iterations per example, with multiple random restarts.

pages.title: The L2, L0, and Linf attacks
pages.subtitle: One framework, three notions of 'small'

blocks.html: Why three attacks. Different threat models care about different notions of “small.” A sensor with bounded noise cares about $\ell_\infty$ (no pixel off by much); an attacker who can only flash a few pixels cares about $\ell_0$ (few pixels touched); a perceptual-similarity argument leans on $\ell_2$. So the paper builds one attack per metric, all sharing the surrogate-$f$ and tanh machinery.

rows: Spreads a faint, smooth perturbation over the whole image; the flagship attack, directly minimizes $\|\delta\|_2$.
How many pixels change at all
Built on the $\ell_2$ attack: iteratively freezes the least-important pixels, shrinking the set that is allowed to change.
Penalizes a shrinking threshold $\tau$: any pixel exceeding $\tau$ is pushed down; $\tau$ is reduced until it cannot go lower.

blocks.html: The $\ell_0$ trick. The $\ell_0$ count is non-differentiable (it is just “how many are nonzero”), so you cannot minimize it directly. The authors run the $\ell_2$ attack, look at which pixels' changes matter least (small gradient × value), freeze those to the clean value, and repeat. Each round shrinks the modifiable set until only a small critical core remains — a clean greedy reduction.

The $\ell_\infty$ trick. The naive objective $\|\delta\|_\infty$ only has a gradient on the single largest pixel, so the optimizer plays whack-a-mole. The authors instead penalize $\sum_i \max(0, |\delta_i| - \tau)$ — the total amount by which pixels exceed a cap $\tau$ — and shrink $\tau$ over time. This gives gradient signal from all over-budget pixels at once.

The result. Across all three metrics the attacks find distortions far smaller than FGSM or the older L-BFGS attack — on MNIST and CIFAR the $\ell_2$ changes are often visually undetectable. These attacks became the reference implementations the whole field measured against.

What defensive distillation does. You train a first network, then train a second network to imitate the first's soft probability outputs, using a high softmax temperature $T$ that smooths the probabilities. At deployment, $T$ is set back to 1, which makes the softmax extremely peaked — outputs are essentially 0 or 1. That saturation makes the gradient an attacker sees through the probabilities vanish, so gradient attacks stall. Hence the celebrated drop to a 0.5% attack success rate.

Why C&W walks right through it. The surrogate $f$ operates on the logits $Z$, the scores before the saturating softmax. Distillation flattens the probabilities but the logits still carry a usable gradient. By never touching the softmax output, the attack is simply immune to the trick distillation relies on. (The authors note you sometimes have to handle numerical scaling, but the principle is that direct: attack the logits, not the probabilities.)

The numbers. The C&W attacks succeed 100% of the time on both the undistilled and the distilled networks (MNIST and CIFAR), and distillation increases the required distortion only marginally — nowhere near enough to call it a defense. The reported robustness was an artifact of testing against attacks that happened to depend on softmax gradients.

The general lesson. A defense that merely hides or flattens gradients can look extremely robust against weak attacks while offering no real protection. This phenomenon — later named gradient masking / obfuscated gradients — is exactly what the Athalye, Carlini & Wagner paper (also in this collection) would systematize a year later.

The figures to picture. The paper shows full target-class grids: a single source digit (say a “7”) turned into every one of the other nine MNIST classes, each with a barely-perceptible perturbation. The $\ell_2$ and $\ell_\infty$ versions look essentially identical to the original to a human; the $\ell_0$ version changes only a handful of pixels but those changes are more visible as scattered dots.

Transferability and $\kappa$. The confidence margin $\kappa$ from the objective is the lever for black-box attacks. With $\kappa = 0$ the examples are minimal-distortion but fragile — they barely cross the boundary, so they often fail to transfer to a different model. Cranking $\kappa$ up pushes them deep into the target region; the paper shows these high-confidence examples transfer to other networks at much higher rates, at the price of larger, sometimes visible, distortion. This trade-off is the bridge from white-box to black-box attacks.

Why it matters. The same example, the same source digit, the same machinery, dialed from “invisible but model-specific” to “visible but universal” with one parameter — this made $\kappa$ a standard tool and showed that minimal distortion and transferability are genuinely in tension.

pages.title: Why this became the benchmark
pages.subtitle: Strong attacks as a measuring instrument

items: It established that minimum-distortion attacks (how little is needed to fool the model), not one-shot attacks, are the right yardstick for robustness.
The logit-based surrogate, binary search over $c$, and tanh reparameterization became standard tools in nearly every later attack.
The confidence parameter $\kappa$ gave a clean knob for trading distortion against transferability — the basis of many black-box attacks.
The C&W $\ell_2$ attack became the default sanity check: a defense that does not survive it is not considered robust.

blocks.html: The shift in standards. By showing a celebrated defense collapse completely under a properly designed attack, the paper changed the standard of evidence in the field. From then on, claiming robustness meant surviving strong, adaptive, optimization-based attacks — and C&W was the attack everyone reached for first.

How it connects. FGSM gave the field its first cheap attack; C&W gave it the gold-standard strong attack; PGD (Madry et al.) gave a robust training method evaluated against strong attacks; and obfuscated gradients turned C&W's “attack the logits, not the gradients you're shown” insight into a general recipe for breaking masked-gradient defenses. This paper is the methodological hinge between them.
Defensive distillation does not significantly increase the robustness of neural networks.
